title: 38 U.S.C. 3709, Refinancing of housing loans (recoupment, net tangible benefit, loan seasoning)
note: The federal anti-churning conditions for VA refinances. Subsection (a) requires the lender to certify a recoupment period and that all fees and incurred costs are scheduled to be recouped on or before 36 months after loan issuance. Subsection (b) requires a net tangible benefit test, a rate not less than 50 basis points below the previous loan where a fixed rate replaces a fixed rate and 200 basis points where an adjustable rate replaces a fixed rate, and limits how discount points may produce the lower rate. Subsection (c) is the seasoning rule. Enacted as section 309 of Pub. L. 115-174, the Protecting Veterans from Predatory Lending Act, May 24 2018; seasoning amended by Pub. L. 116-33, July 25 2019, to measure 210 days from the first payment DUE date. The IRRRL audit worksheet verified this citation against law.cornell.edu on 2026-06-11; subsections (a), (b) and (c) re-read and confirmed verbatim 2026-08-21.

title: 24 CFR 5.609, Annual income
publisher: Electronic Code of Federal Regulations, National Archives
note: The income definition AMI-based federal housing programs run on. STRUCTURE MATTERS: (a) defines annual income as "all amounts, not specifically excluded in paragraph (b)", so (b) is an EXCLUSION LIST and anything absent from it counts. (b)(16) excludes only DEFERRED VA disability benefits "received in a lump sum amount or in prospective monthly amounts." (b)(17) excludes only "[p]ayments related to aid and attendance under 38 U.S.C. 1521 to veterans in need of regular aid and attendance." ONGOING REGULAR SERVICE-CONNECTED DISABILITY COMPENSATION IS NOT IN (b), so under (a) it is counted as annual income. SEARCH BEHIND THAT ABSENCE, named per P33: the corpus is the full text of 5.609(b) as published at the eCFR URL in this row, read on 2026-08-24; the terms looked for were veteran, veterans, VA, service-connected, disability, compensation, 38 U.S.C., aid and attendance, and pension. Neither describes ongoing monthly service-connected compensation. This is an absence within ONE NAMED REGULATION, not across a corpus of documents. title: Housing First or Treatment First? Evidence from the VA's homelessness programs
publisher: Sydney Costantini, Yale University Department of Economics
note: Working paper dated November 2025, posted in the January 2026 folder on the Yale economics site. Population: nearly 300,000 unhoused VETERANS WITH MENTAL ILLNESS who contacted VA homelessness services between April 2011 and February 2017, followed three years, using VA's Homelessness Registry linked to clinical records and mortality data. Compares HUD-VASH, permanent vouchers with optional case management, against Grant and Per Diem, transitional housing with REQUIRED treatment. Two-instrument instrumental variables design using quasi-random variation in voucher availability at clinic arrival and in transitional-housing liaison availability during intake week. FINDINGS VERBATIM: "Housing First reduces three-year mortality by 4.6 percentage points relative to a no-program counterfactual. In contrast, Treatment First has no long-term effects on health." And: "I can statistically rule out that Treatment First is as effective as Housing First at reducing mortality" (F = 4.06; p-value = 0.044). Housing First was also cost-saving, causing substitution away from lengthy inpatient stays. WHY THIS ROW EXISTS: it tests HUD's stated reason at S220, that housing alone cannot solve a crisis driven by addiction and mental illness, ON EXACTLY THAT POPULATION in VA's own programs. SCOPE LIMIT, and it is published on the page: this paper does NOT address HUD's separate aggregate claim that homelessness rose while money was spent. Do not stretch it to that. TIER: working paper, not yet peer-reviewed as far as this project has established; day of month not given, hence PENDING DATE, not guessed.

title: Powers v. McDonough, No. 2:22-cv-08357 (C.D. Cal.), veterans housing at the West Los Angeles VA campus

A federal court has found that mechanism discriminatory in a VA housing context. IT IS CITED FOR THAT PARALLEL AND NOTHING WIDER.
